chapter: Queens Terrace, Decca records and Amen
title: McGuinney's in Sheepshead Bay and not getting Amen royalties
summary: Amen is famous by summer 1942, but Mayo Williams's threats keep Mosley from claiming and he gets no royalties.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: You went to Hollywood?
No, no, I didn't go to Hollywood until '43.
The summer of '42 I went in McGuinney's in Sheepshead Bay.
McGuinney's in Sheepshead bay?
Yeah.
No kidding?
In Sheepshead Bay.
Yeah, yeah, that's a famous place.
Did they have live music there before?
Yeah.
Bob Field's family owned that place; he owns it now himself.
Bob Field?
Bob Field owns that place.
No kidding?
That's who whatchamacallit told me to get in touch with, but I never could do any business with him.
We went in there and by that time "Amen" had gotten famous, it was very famous then, and also Woody Herman had put it in a picture called "What's Cooking".
So therefore, that tune would have been worth some money at that point, I would expect?
That tune was worth a gang of thousands.
So why didn't you put in a claim right then and there with those guys who were all around?
I was afraid of them not recording me. Mayo Williams put the fear of death in me, which was stupid.
He didn't record you anymore anyway.
Not for a while; that's why. He said I am getting you recordings and then I didn't talk too much. If you ask why I didn't record, that is the reason.
Did you get any royalties on these records?
I didn't get a nickel on any of them.
Never, at any time?
Never at any time. That's the point of being what you
call a bad manager. I just loved to play music and that's all I had my mind on.
As long as you got a decent taste on the job--you usually got a pretty good taste of money on the job when you were playing.
